segments.title: Compare warships against their intended mission
segments.summary: A ship's gun size, speed, range, and armour are not a verdict by themselves: begin with the job its navy needed it to perform.
segments.body: Warship comparison cannot be reduced to isolated statistics. Bigger guns, greater speed, longer range, or heavier armour matter only in relation to the task. The insulation analogy shows how something suited to one setting can be the wrong choice in another. The same principle applies between navies and among ships within one navy. Start with the intended mission and role, then ask how effectively the ship performed them. This judges a design by the operational problem it was meant to solve instead of ranking specifications in a league table.

evidence.note: The transcript rejects a statistic-only comparison and says to assess the mission and role a ship was supposed to fulfil.

segments.title: The 1930s Town class and countering surface raiders
segments.summary: The Royal Navy's 1930s Town-class cruisers illustrate how a design suited to hunting surface raiders could also have raiding potential of its own.
segments.body: The 1930s Town-class cruiser is presented as a design shaped by the need to counter surface raiders. That requirement produced the characteristics needed to pursue and fight an independently operating opponent. With deliberate irony, the same qualities could also make the ship an effective surface raider. A specification has meaning only in relation to the threat and role behind it. The class's balance of capabilities becomes clearer when viewed this way than through a raw comparison of figures.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the 1930s Royal Navy Town class as a counter-surface-raider design and notes that the same attributes suit raiding.

segments.title: Why ships with the same class name can demand different comparisons
segments.summary: World War I Town-class scouts, World War II cruisers, and Type 26 anti-submarine frigates share a name, not a common mission or a fair statistical comparison.
segments.body: Several British classes called Town show why a familiar name can mislead. The First World War class was intended for scouting, convoy escort, and trade protection, although wartime circumstances could send it hunting. Its designers did not expect converted merchant ships to fill the raider role they might have to fight. The modern Type 26 Town class is an anti-submarine frigate with a different mission. Direct comparison with either generation of cruiser would erase the operational needs of their eras. A shared class name does not make them a common design category.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the First World War Town class as a scout, convoy escort, and trade-protection ship, then identifies Type 26 as an anti-submarine frigate.

segments.title: Why four super ships may not meet a twelve-ship requirement
segments.summary: A navy needing twelve hulls to cover its positions may be worse served by four expensive super ships, even when each design looks excellent on paper.
segments.body: Warship comparison also has to move from individual performance to fleet-level fit. A ship can have impressive Top Trumps figures and still be a poor answer to its navy's needs. If a nation needs twelve hulls to cover its positions but can afford only four, the expensive super ship leaves tasks uncovered. Cost, quantity, and coverage belong in the assessment alongside speed, range, guns, and armour. A design that looks excellent on paper can still deserve a negative assessment when the nation cannot buy enough ships to fulfil the mission.

evidence.note: The transcript says national requirements and affordability matter, using the example of buying four expensive ships when twelve are needed to cover all positions.
